derivations.quote: Take $\tau=\sigma=1-2^{-50}$, $\beta=1/2$ and $\delta=1/16$.
Take $\lambda'=1-2^{-54}$.
The layer conditions hold with room to spare: $\tau(1+c/\beta)<1-31\cdot2^{-55}<\lambda$. Indeed $\tau(1+c/\beta)=(1-2^{-50})(1+2^{-55})=1-31\cdot2^{-55}-2^{-105}$, while $\lambda=1-8\cdot2^{-55}$.
Also $\sigma+\beta(1-\sigma)=1-2^{-51}<\lambda<\lambda'<1$.
For large $n$ put $b=\lceil\log_2n\rceil$, $p=6b$, $d=\lfloor b^\epsilon\rfloor$.
Put $K=\lfloor d^c\rfloor$.
Take the power of two $T$ in $[4n/b,8n/b)$. Here $T$ is the number of positions of the padded box, an array with $d$ axes, so $Tp=6bT\in[24n,48n)$.

Let $r=2^{\lceil(\log_2T)/d\rceil}$ and $\ell=\log_2r$; choose $d\ell-\log_2T\in[0,d)$ of the axis lengths to be $r/2$ and the others $r$, with the last axis of length $r$. So $\ell$ is the number of address bits of the longest axis, and $r$ is also the record length of the ring. This works because $d\ell\ge\log_2T$ and $d\ell<\log_2T+d$: with $m=d\ell-\log_2T$ axes of length $r/2$ the product is $2^{d\ell-m}=T$, and $m<d$ leaves a last axis of length $r$.
Thus $t_i\in\{r/2,r\}$, $\prod_it_i=T$ and $t_d=r$.

These choices give $Tp=\Theta(n)$, $d=\Theta(p^\epsilon)$, $K=\Theta(p^{\epsilon c})$, $\ell=\Theta(p^{1-\epsilon})$, $r=2^{\Theta(p^{1-\epsilon})}$, so the comparison constants $a_d=a_r=1/12$, $b_d=1$, $b_r=1/3$, $C_\ell=1$ can be fixed for all lengths at once. These are the constants by which the layer and transform lemmas bound $d$, $r$ and $\ell$. They follow from $b/2\le\log_2T\le b$ and $d\le b$, which give $\tfrac1{12}p^\epsilon\le d\le p^\epsilon$ and $\tfrac p{12d}\le\ell\le\tfrac p{3d}$.
Put $\alpha=\lceil(12d^2b)^{1/4}\rceil$.
Put $\gamma=2d\alpha^2$ and $\eta=1/(4d)$. Here $\gamma$ is the total of the $2\alpha^2$-bit scalings of the $d$ axes, and $\eta$ is the relative gap kept between each prime and its power of two.

Since $\lceil A\rceil\le2A$ for $A\ge1$, $\alpha\le2(12d^2b)^{1/4}$, and $8\sqrt{12}<28$. Then $\gamma<28d^2\sqrt b\le28b^{1/2+2\epsilon}\le28b^{2/3}$, so $2\le\alpha<\sqrt p$ eventually and $\gamma=o(b)$.

By the prime-interval lemma, for $0<\eta<1/4$ and $x>e^{2/\eta}$ the interval $(1-2\eta)x<q\le(1-\eta)x$ contains at least $\eta x/(2\log x)$ primes; both $x=r/2$ and $x=r$ qualify since $\log x>8d=2/\eta$, and the count $x/(8d\log x)$ exceeds $d$.
The two intervals are disjoint and each holds more than $d$ primes, so we can choose distinct odd primes with $(1-2\eta)t_i<s_i\le(1-\eta)t_i$; $\gcd(s_i,t_i)=1$ as $t_i$ is a power of two.
Multiplying the lower bounds and applying strict Bernoulli gives $S/T>(1-1/(2d))^d>1/2$ for $d\ge2$, since $(1-x)^d>1-dx$.
With $s_i<t_i$ this gives $T/2<S<T$.
With $\theta_i=t_i/s_i-1\ge\eta/(1-\eta)>\eta$ we get $\alpha^4\theta_i>12d^2b/(4d)=3db\ge6b=p$, the separation hypothesis of the resampling lemma; also $t_i\le r\le T<2^p$.

The deterministic search for the primes takes $n^{o(1)}=o(n)$ time, since its logarithm is $o(p)$ and $p=\Theta(\log n)$; all primes and length parameters are generated by the machine, not given as advice.
